cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(a): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'The Court of Justice of the European Union consists of 27 judges, one from each Member State.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False — the 'Court of Justice of the European Union' is the whole institution, and the 27 judges, one per Member State, sit only in one of its courts, the Court of Justice.
• Art 19(1) TEU: the CJEU includes the Court of Justice, the General Court and specialised courts (Art 257 TFEU; none exists at present).
• Court of Justice: 27 judges plus 11 Advocates General (Art 252(1) TFEU says eight; the Council has raised the number).
• General Court: at least one judge per Member State (Art 19(2) TEU), in fact two per Member State = 54 (Art 48 Statute).
Codex: Art 19(1)–(2) TEU; Arts 252, 254, 257 TFEU; Statute (Protocol No 3) Art 48.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(b): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'Advocates General are members of the Court of Justice who decide on their own those cases that raise no new point of law.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False — Advocates General are members of the Court of Justice, appointed like the judges (Art 253 TFEU), but they never decide a case.
• Role: acting with complete impartiality and independence, the AG makes reasoned submissions in open court to assist the Court (Art 252(2) TFEU). The Opinion does not bind the judges, who often, but not always, follow it.
• Where a case raises no new point of law, the Court may decide, after hearing the AG, to give judgment without an Opinion (Art 20, last paragraph, Statute). The judges still decide.
Codex: Art 19(2) TEU; Arts 252, 253 TFEU; Statute Art 20.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(c): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'To guarantee their independence from national governments, the judges of the Court of Justice are elected by the European Parliament for a single, non-renewable term of five years.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False on every point — judges of the Court of Justice are appointed by common accord of the governments of the Member States, after consulting the Art 255 panel, for a renewable term of six years (Art 19(2) TEU, Art 253 TFEU).
• Criteria: independence beyond doubt and the qualifications for the highest judicial offices, or jurisconsults of recognised competence (Art 253(1)). Partial replacement every three years; reappointment is possible (Art 253(2), (4)).
• Parliament only proposes one of the seven panel members (Art 255(2)). Election by a parliamentary assembly for a single non-renewable (nine-year) term is the ECtHR model, not the EU one.
Codex: Art 19(2) TEU; Arts 253, 255 TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(d): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'Requests for preliminary rulings are always decided by the Court of Justice; the General Court decides all direct actions.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False on both halves — since 1 October 2024 the General Court decides preliminary references in six specific areas (Art 256(3) TFEU, Art 50b Statute), and several direct actions are reserved to the Court of Justice (Art 51 Statute).
• Transferred areas: VAT, excise duties, the Customs Code, tariff classification, passenger rights and emissions trading. The Court of Justice receives every reference, transfers only those falling exclusively within these areas and keeps independent questions of primary law, international law, general principles or the Charter.
• Reserved to the Court of Justice: infringement actions (Arts 258–260), most actions by Member States against acts of Parliament, the European Council or the Council, and actions between institutions.
Codex: Arts 256(1), (3), 267 TFEU; Statute Arts 50b, 51.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(a): Member State Kalmaria has just lost an infringement case before the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice. The Kalmarian government announces that it will appeal against the judgment to the full Court. It also demands that Judge K, the judge of Kalmarian nationality, disclose how he voted and publish a dissenting opinion. Assess both demands. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both fail — the Court of Justice decides at last instance, so there is no appeal, and its deliberations are secret, so there are neither published votes nor dissenting opinions.
• No appeal: appeals lie only against decisions of the General Court (Art 256(1) TFEU, Art 56 Statute), and the full Court is a formation, not a higher court. Kalmaria must comply (Art 260(1) TFEU); revision is possible only on discovery of a new decisive fact (Art 44 Statute).
• Secrecy: the deliberations are and remain secret (Art 35 Statute; oath, Art 2). The judgment is one collegiate decision naming the judges who took part (Art 36), which shields each judge from 'his' government.
Codex: Art 19(2) TEU; Arts 256(1), 260(1) TFEU; Statute Arts 2, 35, 36, 44, 56.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(b): Member State Kalmaria has just lost an infringement case before the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice, against the Opinion of the Advocate General. The Kalmarian government now announces that it will recall Judge K, the judge of Kalmarian nationality, and appoint a judge 'more loyal to Kalmarian interests' for the rest of his term. Can it? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — judges are not delegates of their Member State, and Judge K can be deprived of office only by the unanimous opinion of the judges and Advocates General of the Court of Justice that he no longer meets the conditions or obligations of office (Art 6 Statute).
• Guarantees: independence beyond doubt (Art 19(2) TEU, Art 253 TFEU), oath and immunity (Arts 2, 3 Statute). Before the six-year term ends, office ends only by death, by the judge's own resignation (Art 5 Statute) or under Art 6.
• Kalmaria's only lever is not to propose him again when his term expires; a successor still needs the Art 255 panel's opinion and the common accord of all governments.
Codex: Art 19(2) TEU; Arts 253, 255 TFEU; Statute Arts 2, 3, 5, 6.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(c): Member State Kalmaria, which recently lost an infringement case before the Court of Justice, is now the defendant in a new infringement action brought by the Commission. The case has been assigned to a chamber of five judges. Kalmaria requests that the case be heard by the Grand Chamber and that the judge of Kalmarian nationality sit in it. Must the Court comply? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Partly — the Court must sit as a Grand Chamber because a Member State that is a party has requested it (Art 16, third paragraph, Statute), but Kalmaria cannot demand that its judge sit (Art 18, last paragraph, Statute).
• Grand Chamber: 15 judges, presided over by the President of the Court; its decisions are valid only if 11 judges sit (Arts 16, 17 Statute; Art 251 TFEU).
• A party may not seek a change in the composition of the Court or a chamber because of a judge's nationality or the absence of a judge of its nationality: the Court is not a body of national delegates.
Codex: Art 251 TFEU; Statute Arts 16–18.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(a): The Data Centre Directive (fictitious), adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, had to be transposed by 1 July 2025. Member State Ostravia has notified no transposing measures to the Commission. What must the Commission do before it can bring Ostravia before the Court of Justice, and why does this stage matter? Must the Commission show a specific interest or that the delay has caused harm? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Commission must first complete the pre-litigation procedure of Art 258 TFEU — a letter of formal notice giving Ostravia the opportunity to submit its observations, then a reasoned opinion with a deadline — and it needs to show neither a specific interest nor harm.
• Only if Ostravia does not comply within the period laid down in the reasoned opinion may the case go to the Court of Justice (Art 258(2)). Informal contacts usually come first.
• Why it matters: Ostravia can comply or defend itself, and the stage fixes the subject-matter. The application may not add complaints absent from the letter of formal notice and the reasoned opinion, and the breach is assessed at the end of the reasoned-opinion period.
• As guardian of the Treaties (Art 17(1) TEU) the Commission acts in the general interest. The procedure is objective, so neither a specific interest (Commission v Germany, C-431/92) nor damage is required, and the Commission has discretion whether and when to act (Star Fruit, 247/87).
Codex: Art 17(1) TEU; Art 258 TFEU · Cases: Commission v Germany (C-431/92), Star Fruit (247/87).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(b): The Data Centre Directive (fictitious), adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, had to be transposed by 1 July 2025. Member State Ostravia has notified no transposing measures, and the Commission has started infringement proceedings. Ostravia's government defends itself by arguing (1) that early parliamentary elections prevented the adoption of the transposing act, (2) that building law falls within the competence of its regions, three of which have not yet legislated, and (3) that two other Member States have not transposed the Directive either. Assess these arguments. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: None of the arguments is a defence, because failure to transpose is an objective breach of Art 288(3) TFEU and Art 4(3) TEU that internal circumstances and other states' breaches cannot justify.
• (1) Elections: under settled case law a Member State may not plead provisions, practices or circumstances of its internal legal order to justify non-compliance. The transposition period exists to plan around such events, and fault is irrelevant.
• (2) Regions: the state answers for all its organs, including autonomous regions and their parliaments. The internal division of competences is irrelevant under Art 258.
• (3) Reciprocity: EU law excludes the international-law exceptio non adimpleti contractus. A Member State cannot rely on other states' breaches (Commission v Luxembourg and Belgium, 90 and 91/63) or take unilateral corrective measures (Hedley Lomas, C-5/94); those breaches are pursued separately.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Arts 258, 288(3), 291(1) TFEU · Cases: Commission v Luxembourg and Belgium (90 and 91/63), Hedley Lomas (C-5/94).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(c): The Data Centre Directive (fictitious), adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, had to be transposed by 1 July 2025. Member State Ostravia has notified no transposing measures. Neighbouring Member State Westmark, whose data-centre operators compete with Ostravian ones, wants to act itself. It is considering bringing the dispute before an international arbitral tribunal, or else suing Ostravia before the Court of Justice. Advise Westmark. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Arbitration is excluded by Art 344 TFEU, but Westmark may sue Ostravia before the Court of Justice under Art 259 TFEU after first bringing the matter before the Commission.
• Art 344: Member States may not submit a dispute on the interpretation or application of the Treaties to any other method of settlement (Commission v Ireland, MOX Plant, C-459/03).
• Art 259: the Commission hears both states, orally and in writing, and delivers a reasoned opinion. Whatever it says, or if it delivers none within three months, Westmark may then go to the Court.
Codex: Arts 259, 344 TFEU · Case: Commission v Ireland (MOX Plant, C-459/03).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(d): The Data Centre Directive (fictitious), adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, had to be transposed by 1 July 2025. Member State Ostravia has notified no transposing measures, and the deadline in the Commission's reasoned opinion has expired. The Commission brings the case before the Court of Justice and asks it to impose a lump sum and a daily penalty payment already in this first judgment. (i) Is that possible? (ii) What changes if Ostravia fully transposes the Directive after the reasoned-opinion deadline but before the judgment? (iii) What could the Commission do if a judgment without financial sanctions were simply ignored? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (i) Yes, under Art 260(3) TFEU; (ii) the breach is still declared, but only a lump sum, not a penalty payment, remains appropriate; (iii) a second action under Art 260(2).
• (i) Ostravia has notified no measures transposing a directive adopted under a legislative procedure (Art 289(3)), so already in the Art 258 judgment the Court may impose a lump sum and/or penalty payment up to the amount the Commission specified, payable from the date the Court sets. This covers total and partial non-notification (Commission v Belgium, C-543/17), not incorrect transposition.
• (ii) The breach is assessed at the end of the reasoned-opinion period, so the action does not become devoid of purpose. A penalty payment is coercive and lapses once the breach has ended; a lump sum punishes the past breach and may still be imposed (Commission v Romania, C-549/18).
• (iii) Ostravia must comply with the judgment (Art 260(1)). If it does not, the Commission sends a letter of formal notice (no reasoned opinion is needed), refers the case back and proposes an amount, by which the Court is not bound (Art 260(2)).
Codex: Arts 258, 260(1)–(3), 289(3) TFEU · Cases: Commission v Belgium (C-543/17), Commission v Romania (C-549/18).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(a): Case exercise. Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious), adopted in 2019 by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, active substances may be used in plant protection products only while they are approved. The Commission decides on the renewal of an approval by implementing regulation after a scientific assessment by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). Before deciding, it must give the applicants for renewal the opportunity to comment on EFSA's conclusions. If renewal is refused, the Member States must withdraw all national authorisations of products containing the substance within six months. Feldmann GmbH, an Austrian manufacturer of trivolan, was one of three companies that jointly applied in 2023 for renewal of the approval of the active substance trivolan. In December 2025 EFSA concluded that trivolan is potentially endocrine-disrupting. Without forwarding EFSA's conclusions to the applicants, the Commission adopted an implementing regulation on 12 March 2026 refusing the renewal (the 'Trivolan Regulation'). It was published in the Official Journal on 16 March 2026. Gartenwelt AG, a chain of garden centres that sells many products containing trivolan, is also affected. Both Feldmann and Gartenwelt want to bring an action for annulment against the Trivolan Regulation. Do they have standing? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Feldmann has standing, because the Trivolan Regulation is of direct and individual concern to it as one of the three applicants for renewal (Art 263(4), second limb, TFEU), whereas Gartenwelt, affected only as one of an open class of retailers, has none and must go through the national courts.
• Act and applicants: a binding Commission implementing regulation is reviewable (Art 263(1)). Both companies are non-privileged and neither is an addressee, so each needs the second or third limb of Art 263(4).
• Third limb: as a non-legislative act of general application the regulation is a 'regulatory act' (Inuit, C-583/11 P). But its consequences for the products are given effect by national withdrawals of authorisations, which count as implementing measures even if purely mechanical (T&L Sugars, C-456/13 P), judged from the applicant's position (Telefónica, C-274/12 P). The limb is doubtful, so Feldmann should rely on the second.
• Direct concern (Dreyfus, C-386/96 P): the regulation itself refuses Feldmann's application, and the Member States must withdraw the authorisations without any discretion, so implementation is automatic.
• Individual concern (Plaumann, 25/62): Feldmann belongs to a closed group of three applicants fixed before adoption, and the basic regulation gave it a procedural guarantee in the procedure leading to the act, the right to comment (cf. Timex, 264/82; Cofaz, 169/84). It is distinguished just like an addressee, so its action is admissible if brought in time.
• Gartenwelt: even if directly concerned, it is affected only in its objective capacity as a retailer, since anyone may sell such products, so it is not individually concerned. It must challenge a national measure applying the ban, plead invalidity and ask the court to refer (Art 267). Only the CJEU can declare the regulation invalid (Foto-Frost, 314/85), and the Member States must provide such remedies (Art 19(1), second subparagraph, TEU; UPA, C-50/00 P).
Codex: Arts 263(1), (4), 267, 291(2) TFEU; Art 19(1) TEU · Cases: Plaumann (25/62), Inuit (C-583/11 P), T&L Sugars (C-456/13 P), Telefónica (C-274/12 P), Dreyfus (C-386/96 P), Timex (264/82), Cofaz (169/84), Foto-Frost (314/85), UPA (C-50/00 P).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(b): Case exercise. Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious, adopted in 2019 by Parliament and Council), the Commission decides on the renewal of approvals of active substances by implementing regulation. Feldmann GmbH, an Austrian manufacturer of trivolan, was one of three joint applicants for renewal of the approval of the substance trivolan. On 12 March 2026 the Commission adopted an implementing regulation refusing the renewal (the 'Trivolan Regulation'). It was published in the Official Journal on 16 March 2026. On 13 March 2026 Feldmann's in-house lawyer received an informal e-mail from the Commission's services informing the company of the regulation. She believes that an action for annulment had to be lodged by 13 May 2026. Feldmann's external counsel intends to lodge it on 5 June 2026. Before which court must the action be brought, and is 5 June in time? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Before the General Court, and 5 June 2026 is in time, because the deadline expires at the end of Tuesday 9 June 2026.
• Court: actions by natural or legal persons go at first instance to the General Court (Art 256(1) TFEU, Art 51 Statute).
• Starting point (Art 263(6)): two months from publication, or from notification to the applicant, or, failing both, from the day the applicant learned of the act. Knowledge is only subsidiary. The regulation had to be published (Art 297(2)) and an informal e-mail is not a notification, so time runs from publication on 16 March and the in-house lawyer is wrong.
• Calculation (Rules of Procedure of the General Court, not in the codex): end of the 14th day after publication = 30 March (Art 59); plus two months = 30 May; plus a single 10 days on account of distance (Art 60) = 9 June, a working day. A Saturday, Sunday or official holiday would move the end to the next working day (Art 58(2)).
Codex: Arts 256(1), 263(6), 297(2) TFEU; Statute Art 51 · Rules of Procedure of the General Court Arts 58–60 (not in codex).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(c): Case exercise. Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious, adopted in 2019 by Parliament and Council), the Commission decides on the renewal of approvals of active substances by implementing regulation after an EFSA assessment, and must first give the applicants the opportunity to comment on EFSA's conclusions. The basic regulation governs only the use and marketing of substances within the Union. Feldmann GmbH, one of three joint applicants for renewal of the approval of the substance trivolan, brings an admissible action for annulment against the Commission's implementing regulation of 12 March 2026 refusing renewal (the 'Trivolan Regulation'). It argues: (i) it was never given the opportunity to comment on EFSA's conclusions; (ii) the regulation also prohibits the export of trivolan to third countries; (iii) refusing renewal altogether is disproportionate, because restricting trivolan to use in closed greenhouses would have sufficed. Under which grounds of annulment do these arguments fall, and what are their prospects? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (i) is an infringement of an essential procedural requirement, (ii) lack of competence and (iii) infringement of a rule of law relating to the application of the Treaties (proportionality); (i) and (ii) have good prospects, while (iii) is weaker because of the Commission's wide discretion.
• Art 263(2) TFEU lists four grounds: lack of competence; infringement of an essential procedural requirement; infringement of the Treaties or of any rule of law relating to their application; misuse of powers (not in issue, as nothing suggests an improper purpose).
• (i) The applicants' right to comment under the basic regulation (cf. the right to be heard, Art 41(2)(a) Charter) is an essential procedural requirement. Its breach leads to annulment if it cannot be ruled out that the outcome might have been different. That is likely, because EFSA's conclusions were decisive and Feldmann could have contested them.
• (ii) An implementing act may neither amend nor supplement its basic act (Art 291(2) TFEU). An export ban beyond the basic regulation's scope is ultra vires (Art 13(2) TEU): lack of competence, which can also be pleaded as infringement of the basic regulation. That severable part can be annulled on its own.
• (iii) Proportionality (Art 5(4) TEU; Arts 16–17 Charter) is such a rule of law. But in complex scientific assessments the Commission has wide discretion and may apply the precautionary principle (Art 191(2) TFEU; Pfizer, T-13/99). Only a manifest error or a manifestly inappropriate measure counts, so Feldmann must show that greenhouse-only use would protect health just as well.
Codex: Arts 5(4), 13(2) TEU; Arts 191(2), 263(2), 264, 291(2) TFEU; Arts 16, 17, 41 Charter · Case: Pfizer Animal Health v Council (T-13/99).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(d): Case exercise. Feldmann GmbH, one of three joint applicants for renewal of the approval of the plant protection substance trivolan, brought an action for annulment against the Commission's implementing regulation of 12 March 2026 refusing renewal (the 'Trivolan Regulation'). Following that regulation, the Member States had to withdraw the national authorisations of all products containing trivolan. Assume that on 1 March 2027 the General Court annuls the Trivolan Regulation because the Commission did not give the applicants the opportunity to comment on EFSA's conclusions, as the basic regulation requires. What are the effects of the judgment, from when do they apply, and what must the Commission do? May it simply adopt the same regulation again? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The regulation becomes void ex tunc and erga omnes (Art 264(1) TFEU), but, as a regulation annulled by the General Court, only once the appeal period has expired or an appeal has been dismissed (Art 60 Statute), and the Commission must then cure the defect (Art 266) rather than simply re-adopt the same act.
• Effects: the regulation is treated as never having existed, for everyone (Gartenwelt and farmers included), and the national withdrawals lose their EU basis. The Court may maintain certain effects (Art 264(2)), e.g. to avoid a gap in health protection.
• Timing: by way of derogation from Art 280 TFEU, the annulment takes effect only after the appeal period (two months plus ten days, Art 56 Statute) has run out or an appeal has been dismissed.
• Compliance: Art 266 binds the Commission to the operative part and its supporting grounds. It may resume the procedure where the illegality occurred, hear the applicants on EFSA's conclusions and then decide anew, even refusing again if justified. Re-adopting the identical act without the hearing would breach Art 266.
Codex: Arts 264, 266, 280 TFEU; Statute Arts 56, 60.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(e): Case exercise. Feldmann GmbH, one of three joint applicants for renewal of the approval of the plant protection substance trivolan, has brought an admissible action for annulment before the General Court against the Commission's implementing regulation of 12 March 2026 refusing renewal (the 'Trivolan Regulation'). The refusal is based on Art 4(7) of the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious), adopted in 2019 by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure. Art 4(7) requires refusal whenever a substance is 'potentially' endocrine-disrupting, without any assessment of actual exposure. Feldmann argues that Art 4(7) is itself disproportionate. The Commission replies that the 2019 regulation can no longer be challenged, since the time limit expired long ago, and that a company cannot challenge a legislative act of Parliament and the Council anyway. Assess. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both objections fail — in its pending action Feldmann may plead the illegality of Art 4(7) under Art 277 TFEU notwithstanding the expiry of the Art 263(6) time limit, and if the plea succeeds Art 4(7) is inapplicable in this case and the Trivolan Regulation is annulled for lack of a valid legal basis.
• Conditions: proceedings are pending before the EU courts; the plea targets an act of general application of an institution, which the legislative regulation is; there is a direct legal connection, because the Trivolan Regulation applies Art 4(7); the grounds are those of Art 263(2), here disproportionality.
• Rationale: Art 277 protects parties who could not attack the general act directly (Simmenthal v Commission, 92/78). As one of an open class, Feldmann was not individually concerned by the 2019 legislative regulation, and the regulatory-act limb excludes legislative acts (Inuit), which is exactly why the plea is open to it.
• Effect inter partes only: the 2019 regulation stays in force. Prospects are limited, because given the legislature's wide discretion in health policy only a manifestly inappropriate rule is disproportionate.
Codex: Arts 263(2), (4), (6), 277 TFEU · Cases: Simmenthal v Commission (92/78), Inuit (C-583/11 P).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 4(f): Case exercise. Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious, adopted in 2019 by Parliament and Council), the Commission must adopt an implementing regulation approving or refusing to approve a new active substance within six months of receiving EFSA's conclusions. In 2024 Feldmann GmbH, an Austrian manufacturer of active substances, applied for approval of a new, safer active substance, trivolan-S. EFSA delivered a favourable conclusion in July 2025, but nothing has happened since. By a letter received by the Commission on 2 April 2026, Feldmann formally called on it to decide. By 15 June 2026 the Commission has not replied. What can Feldmann do, until when, and what can it achieve? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Feldmann can bring an action for failure to act under Art 265 TFEU before the General Court by 12 August 2026 at the latest, but it can obtain only a declaration that the Commission's failure to act is unlawful, not the approval itself.
• Admissibility: (1) a duty to act, because the basic regulation required a decision within six months of EFSA's conclusions, i.e. by January 2026; (2) a call to act within a reasonable time (Art 265(2)), the letter received on 2 April 2026; (3) no definition of position within two months, i.e. by 2 June; (4) the action within a further two months (2 August) plus 10 days on account of distance = Wednesday 12 August 2026.
• Standing (Art 265(3)): the wording covers acts the institution failed to 'address' to the applicant, and an approval regulation is general. But Arts 263 and 265 are one and the same remedy, so an individual may also sue over an act that would be of direct and individual concern to it (T. Port, C-68/95), as it would be to Feldmann, the applicant.
• Result: the judgment is declaratory; the Commission must decide (Art 266) and may still refuse. A position defined before judgment, even a negative one, makes the action devoid of purpose, and a refusal is then challenged under Art 263.
Codex: Arts 256(1), 263(4), 265, 266 TFEU · Case: T. Port (C-68/95).
